results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
**How long you must keep tax records**

The IRS requires that you keep any documents that support an item of income or deduction on a returns until the period of limitations for that return expires.  
- **General income‑tax records** – keep them for the period of limitations that applies to your return (usually 3 to 6 years).  
- **Employment‑tax records** – if you have employees, keep all employment‑tax records for at least **4 years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.  
- **Asset‑related records** – keep records relating to property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition.  

These timelines apply unless a longer period is required for other purposes such as insurance or creditor requirements.  
(cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16))

results.question: why do i need to keep business records

**Why do I need to keep business records?**
“Good records will help you do the following.” “Monitor the progress of your business. You need good records to monitor the progress of your business. Good records can increase the likelihood of business success.” “Prepare your financial statements. You need good records to prepare accurate financial statements. results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
The IRS guides you to choose the **cash method** if your business does **not have inventory**.  
In that case, income is reported when it is received and expenses are deducted when they are paid.  
This is the most common choice for many sole‑proprietor small businesses that keep only simple cash‑basis records.

> “Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method because they find it easier to keep cash method records.”  
> [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

If your business **does have inventory**, the general rule is that you must **use an accrual method** for the inventory portion, because accrual accounting properly matches sales with the cost of goods sold.  
You may still use the cash method for other non‑inventory items, but the overall method for inventory must be accrual.

> “If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for sales and purchases, unless you are a small business taxpayer.”  
> [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

A business qualifies as a **small‑business taxpayer** if it has average annual gross receipts of **$31 million or less for the prior three tax years** (indexed for inflation) and is not a tax shelter.

> “You qualify as a small business taxpayer if you (a) have average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the 3 prior tax years (indexed for inflation), and (b) are not a tax shelter.”  
> [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

Once you have selected a method, any change later requires IRS approval (Form 3115 or Form 1128) unless the automatic change procedures apply.

> “After your first return you must generally get IRS approval before you can change to another method.”  
> [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
To identify hazards in your workplace, the handbook recommends doing a routine **self‑inspection**.  

1. **Conduct a self‑inspection** – “An effective way to identify workplace hazards is for knowledgeable and experienced workers to conduct routine safety and health inspections (i.e., self‑inspections). The only way to know if potential hazards exist and if they are under control is to assess work processes directly.”  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

2. **Use the self‑inspection checklist tools** – the handbook’s checklists are “intended … for general industry workplaces … they are a starting point for identifying workplace hazards.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **After checking** – “Small business employers should conduct routine workplace self‑inspections to: •  identify hazards, •  control identified hazards, and •  monitor and evaluate hazard controls to verify that they continue to be effective.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

4. **Compile the results** – “Compile information from your completed checklists with workplace injury and illness records, worker training information, and process and equipment information (e.g., maintenance logs, failure incident reports) to help you determine where challenges exist.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

By following the steps above—using the checklist, recording findings, and reviewing controls—you can systematically check your workplace for hazards.

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
Cash method  
– Income is counted in the tax year you actually **receive** the money.  
– Expenses are counted in the year you actually **pay** them.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

Accrual method  
– Income is counted in the year it is **earned** (when the right to receive it is fixed, even if the cash is received later).  
– Expenses are counted in the year they are **incurred** (even if the cash is paid later).  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes.  The IRS allows a business owner to deduct the ordinary and necessary costs of traveling “away from home” for business, provided the trip meets the two‑step test in the handbook.  **Travel expenses** can be deducted when

- Your duties require you to be away from the general area of your tax home **substantially longer** than an ordinary day’s work, and  
- You need to get sleep or rest to perform your duties while away.  **Travel expenses** includes transportation, baggage fees, parking, tolls, and, if the trip is overnight, meals and lodging (subject to limits).  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

The **Transportation** portion of the same section states that you may deduct the cost of travel by airplane, train, bus or car, as well as fares for taxis, commuting buses or limousines between airport/station and hotel, or from hotel to the work site.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
Executive summaries are the brief opening of a business plan.  According to the SBA Business Planning Guide, the executive summary “should be brief; usually one or two paragraphs, but it should give the reader an overview of what you want to accomplish. For example, describe your idea, how much money you need, what you need it for, how much money you will bring (or have put) into the business, and a brief schedule of your goals. Since you won’t know some of these facts until you complete your business plan, write this section last” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
To describe your target market, the SBA Business Planning Guide tells you to structure the description as follows (see the **Target Market** section on page 14):

- **Define your market niche** – identify the type of customer who is most likely to buy your product or service.  
- **Describe the customer’s characteristics** – break them down by demographics, geography, industry, company size, or the particular problem your product solves.  
- **Estimate the size and growth** of that niche – use population data, sales‑tax figures, industry reports, or other reliable sources to show how large the market is and how quickly it is expanding.  
- **Project the share you will capture** – estimate what percentage of the total market you expect to serve.  

These elements are all required to give a concise, data‑driven picture of the people and businesses you intend to serve:  

> “Describe your market niche; who is your best customer. Identify those customers and describe their characteristics. Business markets might be classified by industry, company size, location, or product use/application. Consumer (household) markets might be segmented by demographics, (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application or benefits sought. Estimate the approximate size and growth potential of the target market(s) using population figures, sales tax info, industry information, etc. Estimate how much of the total market you will capture.”   
>  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

You can then expand this discussion in the marketing section of your business plan under the heading “Target Market.”

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes.  Because your shop is a private business that serves the public, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) classifies it as a **public accommodation**.  Under the ADA, you are required to eliminate physical barriers that are **“readily achievable”** without imposing an undue financial or technical burden.

* “Private businesses that provide goods or services to the public are called public accommodations… If you own, operate, lease, or lease‑to a business that serves the public, then you are covered by the ADA and have obligations for existing facilities… Existing facilities are not exempted by “grandfather provisions” that are often used by building‑code officials. …You must remove physical ‘barriers’ that are ‘readily achievable.’” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

If a barrier is not readily achievable, you must supply an **alternative** service (e.g., mobile service or a separate accessible entrance) that is likewise readily achievable. (ada_guide_small_business.pdf, pages 11‑13)

So, if the steps, entrances, parking, aisles, or counters can be made wheelchair‑accessible without excessive difficulty, you are required to do so.  If doing so is **not** readily achievable, you must provide an alternative service that is readily achievable.



**Sources:**
1. [ada_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 6)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

results.answer:

results.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
results.answer:
**Getting a business up and running**

1. **Decide the legal form of your business** – apply the rules that the **IRS Guidance on “Determining Which Type of Business to Use”** explains:  
   * Sole proprietorship  
   * Partnership  
   * Limited‑liability company (LLC)  
   * Corporation  
   This decision affects your tax reporting, liability, and allowable deductions.  
   (irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 2‑3)

2. **Choose a name and register it if required** – If you operate as a sole proprietor or partnership and do not use the owner’s last name, you must file a fictitious‑name statement (or “doing‑business‑as”) with the state. For corporations or LLCs operating under a name other than the legal name, you must file an assumed‑business‑name statement with the Secretary of State.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)

3. **Apply for a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN)** – Most businesses will need an Employer Identification Number (EIN).  
   * Apply online for immediate issuance.  
   * Mailing or faxing Form SS‑4 takes at least 4 weeks.  
   * The EIN must be used on all returns, statements, and when another person uses your number.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)

4. **Set your accounting period (tax year)** – Choose either a calendar year (Jan 1 – Dec 31) or an alternative 12‑month period.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)

5. **Select an accounting method** – Decide between the *cash method* (expenses when paid, income when received) or the *accrual method* (expenses and income when incurred). The choice determines how you record liabilities, receivables, and depreciation.  
   

---

**Keeping your taxes organized**

| What to keep | Why they matter | Where to find the rule |
|--------------|-----------------|------------------------|
| **Supporting documents** (sales slips, invoices, receipts, bank deposits, canceled checks) | They back every entry in your books and prove the amounts reported on tax returns. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 12 |
| **Business books or journal entries** | They summarize every transaction and provide the basis for income statements, balance sheets, and cash‑flow statements. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 12‑13 |
| **Record‑keeping system (paper or electronic)** | All electronic systems must replicate the accuracy and legibility of hard‑copy books. The IRS may test the system. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 12‑13 |
| **Retention period** | Keep records for the period of limitations on the tax year they support: 3 years for most returns; 4 years for employment‑tax records. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 16 |
| **Year‑end reports** – income statement, balance sheet, cash‑flow, and notes – for managing the business, loan applications, and audit readiness | These documents also complement the **SBA business‑plan** and provide lenders or investors the financial snapshot they need. | sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 16 |

---

**Tax filing basics**

* **Income‑tax return** – As a sole proprietor, file **Form 1040 with Schedule C** (profit or loss from business). As a partnership, LLC, or corporation, use the appropriate form (e.g., 1040‑S, 1120, 1065).  
* **Self‑employment tax** – The same Schedule C returns automatically calculate the SE tax (Form SE).  
* **Estimated payments** – If you expect to owe more than $1 000, make quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040‑ES).  
* **Employment‑tax forms** – If you hire people, you must report wages and payroll taxes (Forms 941, 940, etc.).  
* **Information‑return forms** – Payees of over $600 must receive Form 1099‑MISC, W‑2 for employees, etc.  

(Full list of required federal tax forms and deadlines can be found in **Publication 334 – “Tax Guide for Small Business”**, Chapter 1.)

---

**Putting it all together**

1. Draft a **business plan** (SBA guide – page 4) covering purpose, market, operations, and finances.  
2. File the required state and federal registrations (name, EIN, etc.).  
3. Set up a simple **single‑entry or double‑entry bookkeeping system** (IRS guidance – page 15).  
4. Keep all **supporting documents, journals, ledgers, and bank reconciliations** and store them for the mandated period (IRS – page 12‑16).  
5. Use the records to prepare the required **tax returns** each year, cross‑check them with the financial statements in your plan, and file electronically when convenient (IRS e‑file).

These steps, taken together, provide a clear pathway from the initial idea to a fully organized tax‑ready small business.

results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records

You must keep your tax records for **the length of time that any IRS claim could rely on them**.

> “You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code. For property or asset records, it adds:

2. **Employment‑tax records** – keep for 4 years from the due/paid date.  
3. **Asset‑related records** – keep until the limitation period expires in the year of disposition.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
The IRS documents explain when to use the **cash method** versus the **accrual method** for a new small business.  The choice depends mainly on whether you will keep an inventory and on your level of receipts.

**1. Cash method (simplest for most sole‑proprietors)**
- You can use the cash method if you **do not have an inventory that is necessary to account for your income**.  
- “Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method because they find it easier to keep cash‑method records” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  
- The cash method reports income in the year you receive it and deducts or caps expenses in the year you pay them [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

**2. Accrual method (required if inventory is necessary)**
- If your business produces, purchases, or sells merchandise, you must “keep an inventory and use an accrual method” unless you qualify as a small business taxpayer, in which case you may treat inventory as non‑incidental materials or supplies [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  
- The accrual method reports income in the year it is earned and deducts or caps expenses in the year they are incurred, even if payment is later [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

**3. Small business exception for inventory**
- A small business taxpayer (average annual gross receipts $31 million or less for the 3 prior tax years and not a tax shelter) may keep inventory but still use the cash method on that inventory, treating it as non‑incidental materials or supplies [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).

**Summary for a new small business**
- **If you do not keep inventory** (e.g., you sell services or low‑volume goods that you don’t hold for sale), you should use the **cash method**.  
- **If you keep inventory** that is “necessary to account for your income,” you must use the **accrual method** for those purchases and sales, unless you qualify for the small‐business inventory exception and choose to treat the inventory as non‑incidental materials or supplies (in which case you may still use the cash method for that inventory).

Choose the method that matches your inventory situation and your receipt level, because the IRS requires consistent use of the chosen method and will only allow a change with IRS approval.

They are a starting point for identifying workplace hazards.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Record findings** – Fill out the checklist form (see the sample form on page 9) and include comments on any observed hazard, whether the hazard is controlled, and any actions needed.

4. **Implement controls** – After identifying a hazard, decide on engineering, administrative, or personal‑protective‑equipment controls, as appropriate.  Re‑inspect to verify that the control is still effective.

5. **Monitor and improve** – Periodically repeat the inspection and adjust controls or training as needed.  Keep a record of your inspections, hazard actions, and any training or incident reports.

6. **Seek additional help** – If you need guidance, the handbook lists the OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program as a free, confidential resource that can help you assess and fix hazards. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)

By following these steps and using the self‑inspection checklists, you can systematically spot and eliminate hazards in your workplace.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash and accrual accounting are the two main methods businesses use to record income and expenses for tax purposes.  

**Cash method**  
* Records income when it is actually (or constructively) received.  
* Records expenses when they are actually paid.  
* Example: you receive a $500 check on December 30, 2025, but you cannot deposit it until January 3, 2026; you must include the $500 in income for 2025 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  

**Accrual method**  
* Records income when it is earned, regardless of when it is received.  
* Records expenses when they are incurred (the liability exists), regardless of when they are paid.  
* Example: you buy office supplies in December 2025, receive the bill, but pay in January 2026; you can deduct the expense in 2025 because the liability has been fixed and economic performance has occurred [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  

The key difference is that the cash method ties income and expenses to actual cash flow, while the accrual method ties them to the timing of when the transaction events occur.  

Both methods are allowed, but if your business keeps inventory you must generally use the accrual method for inventory items (unless you qualify as a small‑business taxpayer and meet the specific criteria).[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes.  The IRS allows a business owner to deduct ordinary and necessary expenses that are incurred while traveling away from home for business purposes.  According to *Publication 334*, travel expenses can be deducted when:

1. **You’re traveling away from home.**  
   “Your duties require you to be away from the general area of your tax home … substantially longer than an ordinary day’s work…and you need to get sleep or rest to meet the demands of your work while away from home.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

2. **The expenses are ordinary and necessary.**  
   “These are the ordinary and necessary expenses of traveling away from home for your business.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

3. **You can deduct:**

   * **Transportation** – “You can deduct the cost of travel by airplane, train, bus, or car between your home and your business destination.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  
   * **Taxi, commuter bus, and limousine** – fares between the airport/rail station and your hotel or work site. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  
   * **Baggage and shipping** – costs of sending baggage or items between your regular and temporary work locations. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  
   * **Car or truck** – operating and maintenance costs while traveling away on business.  You may use either actual expenses or the standard mileage rate, plus business‑related tolls and parking. (irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 40‑41)  

4. **Meals and lodging** – “You can deduct the cost of meals and lodging if your business trip is overnight or long enough that you need to stop for sleep or rest to properly perform your duties.”  You may use actual expenses or the standard meal allowance; in most cases only 50 % of the meal expense is deductible. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

5. **Other related expenses** – cleaning, telephone, tips, and certain business‑related parking and tolls for the vehicle. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

Thus, as long as your travel meets the “away from home” criteria and the expenses are ordinary and necessary, you can deduct them on Schedule C (Form 1040) or the appropriate business tax return.

runs.question: how do i describe my target market
runs.answer:
To describe your target market you should follow the steps outlined in the SBA Business Planning Guide:

1. **Define your market niche** – state the specific group of customers that your product or service is best suited for.  
2. **Identify those customers** – describe who they are and what makes them the ideal customer for you.  
3. **Describe their characteristics** – for business markets, categorize by industry, company size, location, or product use; for consumer markets categorize by demographics (age, gender), geography, economic status, lifestyle, product application, or benefits sought.  
4. **Estimate the market size and growth** – use population figures, sales tax info, industry data, etc., to gauge the overall size of the target market and its potential growth.

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes.  If you sell goods or provide services to the public, the ADA requires that your shop be physically accessible unless it is *not readily achievable*.  In practice that means:

* “When a business has two public entrances, in most cases, only one must be accessible” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  
* “Providing physical access to a facility from public sidewalks, public transportation, or parking is basic to making goods and services available to people with disabilities” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  
* If making an entrance accessible is not readily achievable, “an alternative service such as home delivery or other service must be provided, if doing so is readily achievable” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  

So, unless your shop’s layout or budget makes accessibility truly impractical, you are required to make it wheelchair‑accessible.

**Summary**

runs.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
runs.answer:
To start a business and keep its taxes organized, follow the step‑by‑step guidance that the IRS and SBA provide in their own publications.

---

### 1. Decide on a legal structure  

A business’s legal form determines which tax return it must file and what other formalities it must observe.  
The IRS explains this in the first section of *Starting a Business and Keeping Records*:

> “Your form of business determines which income tax return form you have to file…  
>  Sole proprietorships…  
>  Partnerships…  
>  Corporations…”  
> [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=3)

Choose from the common options (sole proprietor, partnership, corporation, LLC, etc.) based on how you want to be taxed and the level of personal liability you are comfortable with.

---

### 2. Obtain the necessary taxpayer identification number (TIN)  

You must provide a TIN on every federal tax return and on information returns you file.  
The IRS book gives the two most common TINs and how to get them:

> “You must have a TIN … Two of the most common kinds of TINs are the social security number (SSN) and the employer identification number (EIN).  
>  EINs are assigned to sole proprietors, LLCs, corporations, and partnerships …”  
> [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)  

Apply for an EIN as early as possible, either online (immediately) or by mailing Form SS‑4 (at least 4 weeks before you need it).

---

### 3. Pick an accounting method  

You must use a single accounting method that “clearly shows your income” for the tax year (cash or accrual).  
The publication states:

> “In general, any accounting method that consistently uses accounting principles suitable for your trade or business clearly shows income.”  
> [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

Your method must be the same for preparing your return and for keeping your books.  
If you later wish to change it, you normally need IRS approval (see Pub. 538).

---

### 4. Set up a record‑keeping system  

The IRS recommends a system that records every business transaction and includes supporting documents.  
It tells you what must appear in the books:

> “Your recordkeeping system should include a summary of your business transactions… Your books must show your gross income, as well as your deductions and credits.”  
> [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

Keep the following materials (the “recordkeeping system example” on page 16 outlines the actual books and folders you should use):

*  Business checkbook  
*  Daily & monthly cash‑receipt summaries  
*  Check‑disbursement journal  
*  Depreciation worksheet  
*  Employee‑compensation record (if you have staff)  

Also keep all supporting documents (invoices, receipts, bank‑deposit slips, canceled checks).  The IRS says:

> “You must keep supporting documents ... These documents contain information you need to record in your books.”  
> [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

---

### 5. Know how long to keep records  

The IRS requires you to keep records “as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code.”  
Typical retention periods are listed in the publication:

> “How Long To Keep Records … You must keep your records … until the period of limitations for that return runs out.”  
> [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

For example, employment‑tax records last 4 years after the tax becomes due; most other records should be kept until the statute of limitations has expired.

---

### 6. File the right tax returns and keep them organized  

Use the *Business Taxes* section of Pub. 583 to know which forms you must file (Schedule C, 1065, 1120, etc.) and when to file them.  
The *Recordkeeping* section (page 11) explains that you should keep these returns and all related documents available for inspection:

> “You must keep your business records available at all times for inspection by the IRS.”  
> [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

Following the IRS guidance above, schedule your tax payments, file information returns for payroll, and maintain an electronic version of the books (the IRS accepts electronic storage if it meets the same requirements as paper).

---

### 7. Use the SBA Business Planning Guide for non‑tax organization  

While the IRS covers tax‑specific steps, the SBA guide teaches you broader business‑planning steps

runs.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
runs.answer:
To keep your employees safe and your premises accessible you must meet the requirements set out in the OSHA Small Business Safety and Health Handbook and the ADA Small Business Guide.  The following are the key items you need to address, with the exact passages that define each requirement:

---

### 1. **Keep the workplace free of recognized hazards (OSHA General Duty Clause)**  
The employer must provide “a place of employment which are free from recognized hazards that are causing or are likely to cause death or serious physical harm to his employees.”  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)

### 2. **Maintain safe walking‑working surfaces**  
* Walk‑working surfaces must be kept clean, orderly, and in a sanitary condition, with holes and spills corrected or repaired, and the surface kept free of slip hazards.  
* All walking‑working surfaces must be inspected regularly and maintained in a safe condition.  
  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)

### 3. **Provide guardrails, fall protection and fall‑hazard controls**  
* Guardrails are required when an aisle, walkway or stairway surface is elevated more than four feet (1.2 m).  
  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)

### 4. **Ensure safe means of access to and egress from walking‑working surfaces**  
* Workers must be provided with a safe means of access to and egress from walking‑working surfaces.  
  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)

### 5. **Ramps and access routes for employees (ADA)**

runs.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
runs.answer:
**What to track when you’re filing business taxes**  
* Track every item that is **income** for the year and every **deductible expense** that the IRS allows you to claim. According to the IRS guide, “You need to keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  
* Keep a copy of every *supporting document*—sales slips, receipts, invoices, bank deposit slips, payroll records, and any other paperwork that shows the source and amount of the income or expense [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  
* For employment‑related taxes, you must keep payroll records and forms such as W‑2, W‑4, 1099, and records of employment taxes for at least 4 years [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  
* If you use a car or truck for business, record mileage and costs for fuel, repairs, tolls, parking, insurance, registration, and any other expenses you plan to deduct [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).  
* For any taxes that must be paid quarterly (e.g., employment, excise), keep a schedule of deposits and the forms you filed [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8).  

**What to track on business travel trips**  
* **Transportation** – keep receipts or logs for airfare, train, bus, taxi, limousine, or car rental, including distances if you use the mileage method [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).  
* **Lodging** – retain hotel receipts or other lodging documents; if the trip is overnight or long enough that you need sleep or rest, you can claim lodging costs [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41).  
* **Meals** – record dates, amounts, and purpose of each meal. For most trips you may deduct 50 % of meal costs [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41).  
* **Transportation costs between the airport/station and the hotel, and between the hotel and the work location** – keep receipts for these local trips [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).  
* **Business‑related tolls, parking, and tips** – keep receipts for these as well [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).  

In short, keep a detailed log or receipts for **income, deductible expenses, payroll and employment records, and any transportation‑related costs** (fuel, tolls, parking) for your business. For travel, maintain **transportation, lodging, meals, and related local‑trip receipts**, and note the purpose of each expense to show it’s ordinary and necessary for your trade or business.

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
You need an EIN only if the IRS requires it for the type of business activity you’ll be doing.  
From the IRS guidance:

* “You must also have an EIN to use as a TIN if you do either of the following:  
  • Pay wages to one or more employees.  
  • File pension or excise tax returns.”  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

If you are a sole proprietor with no employees and you’re fine using your SSN, an EIN is optional; you can still use an SSN as your TIN. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)

The accounting method you use is independent of whether you have an EIN.  When you file your first income‑tax return, you must choose an accounting method—either cash or accrual (or a special method if applicable).  The publication explains:

* “You choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income tax return. There are two basic accounting methods:  
  1. **Cash method** – report income when received and deduct expenses when paid.  
  2. **Accrual method** – report income when earned and deduct or capitalize expenses when incurred.”  
  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

So, an EIN is required only for certain tax or payroll situations, and the accounting method you adopt is a separate decision made when you first file a return, not something that “comes with” an EIN.

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
You must keep your tax records for the time required to satisfy the Internal Revenue Code’s “period of limitations” rules and any specific tax‑type requirements that apply.  

* For most income‑tax items, retain records **as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code**—that is, until the period of limitations for that return ends . [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
* For employment‑tax records, keep them for **at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
* For assets, keep records until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you **dispose of the property in a taxable disposition**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

If other purposes (e.g., insurance or creditor requirements) demand longer retention, do not discard the records until those needs have been checked. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

> "Accounting Methods
> An accounting method is a set of rules used to determine when and how income and expenses are reported. Your accounting method includes not only the overall method of accounting you use, but also the accounting treatment you use for any material item.
> You choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040) for the business. After that, if you want to change your accounting method, you must generally get IRS approval. … Kinds of methods. Generally, you can use any of the following accounting methods.
> • Cash method.

> • Combination method using elements of two or more of the above." [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

The method you pick should also make sense for your business. For example:

* If you have inventory that must be reported to show income, you’re generally required to use an **accrual** method for sales and purchases unless you qualify as a "small business taxpayer" (see the definition of a small business taxpayer in Pub. 583).  
* Most individuals and many sole proprietors who do not keep inventory and who find it easier to keep track of cash flow use the **cash** method.  
* You may combine methods (e.g., cash for most items but accrual for inventory) as long as the combined method clearly reflects your income (see the combination‑method rules on page 16 of the same publication).

So your first‑return choice is the accounting method you will use, and you must continue to use that method on all future returns (unless you obtain IRS approval to change it).

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
Small business employers should conduct routine **workplace self‑inspections**.  
A self‑inspection lets you see whether potential hazards exist and whether they are under control by directly assessing work processes:

- Identify hazards.  
- Control the identified hazards.  
- Monitor and evaluate hazard controls to verify they remain effective.

The handbook provides **self‑inspection checklists** that serve as a starting point for identifying hazards in general‑industry workplaces (not construction or maritime).  The checklists are based on OSHA standards and accepted safety principles, and they help you decide where to begin improving safety and health for your workers.  
  [cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)]

Using these tools – routine self‑inspections guided by the checklists – is the process OSHA recommends for spotting and addressing hazards in your workplace.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash‑method accounting records income and expenses **when money actually changes hands** – you report revenue in the year you receive it and usually deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you pay them.  
Accrual‑method accounting records income and expenses **when they are earned or incurred**, regardless of when cash moves – you report revenue in the year it is earned (even if payment comes later) and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year they are incurred (even if payment comes later).

These are the rules as stated in the IRS guide for starting a business:

[quote] "1. Cash method. Under the cash method, you report income in the tax year you receive it. You usually deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you pay them. 2. Accrual method. Under an accrual method, you generally report income in the tax year you earn it, even though you may receive payment in a later year. You deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you incur them, whether or not you pay them that year." [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes – the IRS allows a sole proprietor (and other self‑employed people) to deduct ordinary and necessary **business‑travel expenses**.

* You can deduct the cost of transportation by airplane, train, bus, or car between your home and the business destination [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).  
* If the trip keeps you away from home long enough that you need sleep or rest to perform your job, the travel is considered “away from home.”  
* Meals and lodging are also deductible: you can deduct actual expenses or a standard meal allowance, but only 50 % of meals is generally allowable [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41).  
* Other deductible items on a business trip include dry‑cleaning, telephone costs, and tips, and you may deduct parking fees or tolls that are business‑related [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41).  

So, yes, you can deduct ordinary and necessary travel expenses incurred while traveling away from home for business, subject to the rules shown above.

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes. As a small retail shop that serves the public, you are considered a **public accommodation** under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).  Existing facilities are **not exempt** from ADA requirements, and you must remove “barriers that are **readily achievable**” in order to allow people who use wheelchairs (or other mobility devices) to enter and use the business. 

🔹 **ADA Requirement for Existing Facilities** – “Existing facilities are not exempted by “grandfather provisions” that are often used by building code officials. … If you own, operate, lease, or lease to a business that serves the public, then you are covered by the ADA and have obligations for existing facilities as well as for compliance when a facility is altered or a new facility is constructed. … You must remove physical “barriers” that are “readily achievable”​ [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)”.

🔹 **Accessible Entrance** – If you cannot make a building entrance accessible, you must provide an alternative accessible means (e.g., a ramp, lift, or another entrance) “if doing so is readily achievable” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  

Therefore, you are required to make your shop wheelchair‑accessible (or provide an accessible entrance or alternate service) unless the modifications are not “readily achievable” given your resources or physical constraints.

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:

|--------|---------|------------------|

[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| OSHA Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report) | Provides detailed information for each recordable case that was entered in Form 300 | **Kept along with the Form 300 log for at least five years**. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| OSHA Form 300A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) | Annual summary of injuries and illnesses for the preceding calendar year | **Kept at the worksite for at least five years**. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| Work‑related fatality, inpatient hospitalization, amputation, or loss‑of‑eye reports | Must be transmitted to OSHA within the required time limits (8 hours for fatalities; 24 hours otherwise) and the records are also kept with the Form 300/301/300A series. | **Same five‑year retention requirement** (see reporting requirements). [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| Medical, exposure, and training records associated with the injuries | Document treatment, exposure, and training that may be required by OSHA standards | Retained **for the time period required for each specific type of record** (e.g., medical records for as long as the employer must keep them). [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

---

**Summary**

1. **Tax**: Keep business books, receipts, invoices, payroll records, and all supporting documents for the period of limitations for the relevant tax return, plus at least 4 years for employment taxes and until the end‑of‑life of the property for asset records.  
2. **Injury/Illness**: Maintain OSHA Forms 300, 301, 300A and any related medical or training paperwork for at least five years at the worksite; report fatalities and serious cases to OSHA within the specified hours/days.  

These retention periods are taken directly from the employer‑handbooks on recordkeeping.

runs.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
runs.answer:
**To keep your employees safe** – follow the OSHA Small‑Business Safety & Health Handbook:

- “Small business employers should conduct routine workplace self‑inspections to:  
  • identify hazards,  
  • control identified hazards, and  
  • monitor and evaluate hazard controls to verify that they continue to be effective.”  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

- “An effective way to identify workplace hazards is for knowledgeable and experienced workers to conduct routine safety and health inspections (i.e., self‑inspections).”  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

- “Manage a safety and health program that includes management leadership, worker participation, hazard identification and assessment, hazard prevention and control, education and training, program evaluation and improvement, and communication and coordination.”  
  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)  

- Consult the OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program for free, confidential help: “The OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program offers no‑cost and confidential occupational safety and health services to small and medium‑sized businesses.”  
  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)

**To keep your premises accessible** – follow the ADA Small‑Business Guide (text with the “readily achievable” standard):

- “If you own or operate a business that serves the public you must remove physical “barriers” that are “readily achievable.””  
  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

- “When parking is provided for the public, designated accessible parking spaces must be provided, if doing so is readily achievable.”  
  [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)  

  *Each accessible parking space must be at least 8 feet (96 in) wide, have a 5‑foot (60 in) wide access aisle, and a vertical clearance of at least 98 in.*

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
You **do need an EIN** if your business files a tax return that requires a separate employer‑identification number.  The IRS says you must get an EIN “if you have employees or pay federal excise tax, a federal employer’s identification number (EIN) must be obtained… If your business will hire employees … a Federal Employer’s Identification Number (EIN) must be obtained from Internal Revenue Service” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4).

A sole proprietor who has no employees may use the owner’s SSN, but the IRS allows, and often encourages, a sole proprietor to obtain an EIN instead of using the SSN for business‑related filings [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4).

The **accounting method** is not tied to the EIN; it is a separate choice you make when you file your first income‑tax return.  The IRS gives you two basic options:

* **Cash method** – You report income in the year you receive it and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you pay them [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  
* **Accrual method** – You report income when you earn it, even if you are not paid until a later year, and you deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you incur them [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

You must choose one method for each business, keep consistent books, and generally need IRS approval to change methods later [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
For a new small‑business owner the IRS gives two basic methods:

* **Cash method** – you record income when you receive it and expenses when you pay them.  
  “Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method because they find it easier to keep cash‑method records.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

* **Accrual method** – you record income when you earn it and expenses when they are incurred, even if the money is not yet received or paid.  “Under an accrual method, you generally report income in the tax year you earn it, even though you may receive payment in a later year.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

Which one you should use depends on whether your business has inventory:

*If you **do not** keep inventory, the small‑business exception allows you to use the cash method.  
“If you are a small business taxpayer, you can choose not to keep an inventory, but you must still use a method of accounting for inventory that clearly reflects income.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

*If you **do** keep inventory, you generally must use the accrual method for purchases and sales of that inventory, and you cannot use the cash method for those items.  
“…you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for your purchases and sales.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

So:

- **No inventory → Cash method** (easier to keep).  
- **Inventory → Accrual method** for inventory items; you may still use cash for other items if the small‑business rule is satisfied.

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To identify and manage hazards in your workplace, follow the routine self‑inspection process described in the OSHA Small Business Safety and Health Handbook.  

1. **Plan and schedule regular inspections**  
 • Conduct inspections routinely (e.g., weekly, monthly) as the handbook recommends routine self‑inspections.  
 • Involve knowledgeable and experienced workers so the inspection covers all key work areas.  

2. **Use the handbook’s self‑inspection checklists** – a practical tool for finding hazards.  
 • The first page of each checklist (see the sample on page 9) starts with basic information (company name, worksite, work area) and then lists items such as *Safety and Health Programs*, *General Work Environment and Housekeeping*, *Emergency Action Plans*, *Electrical Safety*, etc.  
 • For each item, mark “Yes/No/N/A” and add comments so you record whether a hazard is present and any observations.  

3. **Identify, control, and monitor hazards**  
 • The handbook says: “Small business employers should conduct routine workplace self‑inspections to: • identify hazards, • control identified hazards, and • monitor and evaluate hazard controls to verify that they continue to be effective.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  
 • After you note a hazard, decide on a control (engineering, administrative, or PPE) and implement it.  
 • Re‑inspect the same area to confirm that the control is working.  

4. **Compile and use supporting information**  
 • Combine checklist results with injury/illness logs, training records, maintenance logs, and incident reports to see patterns and prioritize action.  
 • The handbook also suggests reviewing OSHA standards and other resources for specific hazard controls [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).  

5. **Seek help if needed**

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash vs. accrual accounting are the two main methods the IRS allows a business to use to match income and expenses on its tax return.

**Cash method**  
Under the cash method you report income in the tax year you **receive** it, and you normally deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you **pay** them.

**Accrual method**  
Under an accrual method you generally report income in the tax year you **earn** it—even if you receive the payment later—and you deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you **incur** them, whether or not you pay them that year.

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes.  The IRS allows a taxpayer who is a small‑business owner to deduct the ordinary and necessary expenses that are incurred while traveling away from home for business.  The deduction is available for transportation, lodging, meals, baggage, parking, tolls, and other related costs, subject to the rules set out in the *Publication 334, Small‑Business Tax Guide*.

*  **Travel qualification** – You can deduct travel expenses only when you are “traveling away from home” *if both of the following are true* (IRS Pub. 334, page 40):

   1. “Your duties require you to be away from the general area of your tax home substantially longer than an ordinary day’s work.”
   2. “You need to get sleep or rest to meet the demands of your work while away from home.”【irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 40】

*  **Transportation** – The cost of travel by airplane, train, bus, or car *between your home and your business destination* is deductible (IRS Pub. 334, page 40).

*  **Lodging** – If the trip is overnight or long enough that you need sleep, you may deduct the cost of lodging (IRS Pub. 334, page 41).

*  **Meals** – You may deduct the cost of meals if the trip is overnight or long enough.  You can use actual expenses or a standard meal allowance, but *in most cases you can deduct only 50 % of your meal expenses* (IRS Pub. 334, page 41).

*  **Other related costs** – Baggage, shipping, parking fees, and tolls are also deductible (IRS Pub. 334, page 41).

These expenses are entered on Schedule C (Form 1040) for a sole proprietor or the appropriate business‑tax form.  The rules in the publication provide further detail on how to apportion the deduction when the vehicle or other items are used for both business and personal purposes.

In short, you can deduct ordinary and necessary business travel expenses that meet the “away from home” criteria, with meals limited to 50 % and transportation, lodging, and related costs deductible as outlined above.

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes.  The **Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)** requires that a small business that is open to the public make its premises reasonably accessible to people with disabilities.  The ADA Small Business Guide explains the specific elements that must be provided, or a reasonable alternative that is “readily achievable.”

**1. Accessible entrance**

* If the shop has two or more entrances, only one must be accessible.  
  *A shop with an accessible entrance on one side can use that entrance even though the sidewalk entrance is not accessible, provided a sign directs customers to it.*  
  (isa: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10))

* Where a step exists, make it an accessible entrance by adding a ramp or modifying the step.  
  *The ramp slope must be no steeper than 1:12, and handrails are required when the slope is steeper than 1:20 and the vertical rise exceeds 6 inches.*  
  (isa: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10))

**2. Doorways and hardware**

* Doors should be at least 36 inches wide when fully opened.  
  (isa: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12))

* Door hardware must be accessible (lever handles, loop‑type handles, etc.) and not require tight grasping.  
  (isa: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12))

**3. Parking**

* When public parking is offered, at least one accessible parking space must be provided and an accessible route must exist between the space and the accessible entrance.  
  (isa: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8))

**4. Interior accessibility**

* Sales and service counters at least 36 inches long and no higher than 36 inches above the floor must be available, with a 30 × 48‑inch clear space in front of the counter to allow wheelchair maneuvering.  
  (isa: [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15))

* A minimum of 36‑inch wide aisles, turn‑around spaces (≥ 3 ft), and accessible routes to all service areas must be maintained when “readily achievable.”  
  (isa: [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14))

**5. Alternatives**

* If any element cannot be implemented “readily achievable,” a reasonable alternative (e.g., staff assistance, auxiliary counters, accessible signaling) may be used.  
  (isa: [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15))

In short, if your shop is open to the public, you must provide an accessible entrance, accessible parking, and interior accessibility features such as accessible doors, counters, and aisles, or otherwise offer equally effective alternatives that are readily achievable.

runs.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
runs.answer:
**Record‑keeping for federal tax purposes (IRS Publication 583)**  

- **General retention rule** – You must keep records that support an item of income or a deduction on a return **until the period of limitation for that return runs out**. The period of limitation is the time during which the IRS can assess additional tax or you can amend the return (Table 3, page 16).  
  *[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)]*  

- **Employment‑tax records** – If you have employees you must keep all employment‑tax records for **at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)]*  

- **Supporting documents for business transactions** – Keep sales slips, paid bills, invoices, receipts, deposit slips, canceled checks, and other documents that support the entries in your books and on your tax return.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)]*  

**Record‑keeping for work‑site injuries and illnesses (OSHA Small‑Business Safety & Health Handbook)**  

- **OSHA Forms 300, 301, and 300A** – Records of all work‑related injuries and illnesses (except minor first‑aid cases) are kept at the worksite for **at least five years**.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)]*  

- **Worker medical and exposure records** – Retain them for the time period required for each specific type of record (e.g., medical treatment records, exposure records).  
  *[cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)]*  

- **Worker training records** – Must be kept and be accessible to workers as required by OSHA standards (the handbook does not give a fixed shelf‑life, but they must be available whenever requested).  
  *[cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)]*  

- **Fatality and severe‑injury reporting** – All work‑related fatalities must be reported to OSHA within **8 hours**; in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye must be reported within **24 hours**.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)]*  

---  

**Summary**

| Purpose | Record Type | Minimum Retention Period |
|---------|-------------|--------------------------|
| Federal tax records | Documents supporting income or deductions (receipts, invoices, bank statements, etc.) | Until the period of limitation for that tax return (see Table 3) |
| Federal tax records | Employment‑tax records | 4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid |
| OSHA injury/illness | OSHA Form 300 (log), 301 (incident report), 300A (summary) | 5 years |
| OSHA injury/illness | Worker medical and exposure records | As required for each specific record type |
| OSHA injury/illness | Worker training records | Whenever required by OSHA (must be accessible) |

These are the only retention periods specified in the documents you have. If your business has other specific record‑keeping obligations (e.g., state taxes, industry‑specific reporting), those are not covered in the documents cited.

runs.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
runs.answer:
**1. Writing a Business Plan**

The Small Business Administration’s “Business Planning Guide” describes the process and the structure you should follow.  
* First, explain why a plan is needed and create a clear outline.  
  * “Developing a business plan is the first step to a successful business…” – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
  * The guide lists the key sections: Cover Page, Table of Contents, Executive Summary, Business, Management, Market, Money, and Exhibits – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

* **Cover Page** – include company name, address, phone number, owners and date. – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
* **Executive Summary** – a brief overview of the idea, financing needs, and goals (write last). – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
* **Business** – describe the industry, your product/service, competitive advantage, licenses, facilities, and equipment. – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  
* **Management** – outline the organizational structure and key personnel. – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  
* **Market** – identify target customers, market size, growth, and competition. – [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)  
* **Money** – include financial projections and startup costs. The guide lists the specific documents you should prepare:  
  * Summary of Financial Need, 3‑Year Income Projection, Statement of Cash Flow, Balance Sheet, Break‑even Analysis – [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  
  * Pointers on preparing these items can be found in the “Instructions for Preparing Projected Financial Statements” section on page 17 –   
* **Exhibits** – attach resumes, contracts, floor plans, etc. – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

Follow the guide’s Business Plan Outline on page 4 to ensure each part of the plan is complete and well‑organized.

---

**2. Setting Up Accounting for a New Business**

The IRS *Publication 583 – Starting a Business* explains how to establish a bookkeeping system and choose an accounting method.

* **Choose an Accounting Method** – you decide with the first income‑tax return.  
  * “You choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income tax return.” – [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
  * Two basic methods: Cash (“you report income when you receive it… deduct expenses when you pay them”) – [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
    and Accrual (“you report income when you earn it… deduct expenses when you incur them”). – [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

* **Open a Business Checking Account** – keep business and personal accounts separate.  
  * “One of the first things you should do when you start a business is open a business checking account.” – [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

* **Recordkeeping Foundations** – record expenses when they occur, keep receipts, and note the source of each deposit.  
  * “Record expenses when they occur, and identify the source of recorded receipts.” – [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

* **Bookkeeping System** – decide between single‑entry or double‑entry.  
  * Single‑entry is based on an income statement and uses a daily summary of cash receipts and a monthly summary of cash receipts and disbursements – [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)  
  * Double‑entry uses journals and ledgers, and provides built‑in checks and balances. Each account has a debits side and a credits side. – [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)

* **Reconcile Monthly** – compare bank statements, checkbooks, and ledgers to catch errors.  
  * “You should reconcile your checking account each month.” – [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

* **Keep Detailed Records** – use a business checkbook, daily cash receipt summaries, and a check‑disbursement journal.  
  * “The business checkbook is the basic source of information for recording your business expenses.” – [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  
  * “You also use a daily summary of cash receipts… and a monthly summary of cash receipts and disbursements.” – [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)

Follow these steps to establish a reliable accounting foundation that will support accurate financial reporting, tax compliance, and business decision‑making.

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
**Do you need an EIN?**  
- The IRS says you must have a taxpayer identification number (TIN) so it can process your returns.  An EIN is issued to *sole proprietors, partnerships, corporations, and other entities* by the IRS and is required if you *pay wages to one or more employees* or *file pension or excise tax returns*【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 4】【irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 6】.  

**Which accounting method is used with an EIN?**  
- When you file your first income‑tax return, you choose an accounting method.  The IRS offers two basic methods:  
  1. **Cash method** – report income when you receive it and deduct or capitalize expenses when you pay them.  
  2. **Accrual method** – report income in the year it is earned, even if payment is received later; deduct or capitalize expenses when they are incurred.  
- A small‑business taxpayer may use the cash method unless inventory is required, in which case an accrual method is generally required【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 5】.  

These are the rules the documents provide about needing an EIN and the accounting methods that can be used with it.

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
**How long you must keep tax records**

The IRS requires that you keep any documents that support an item of income or deduction on a returns until the period of limitations for that return expires.  
- **General income‑tax records** – keep them for the period of limitations that applies to your return (usually 3 to 6 years).  
- **Employment‑tax records** – if you have employees, keep all employment‑tax records for at least **4 years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.  
- **Asset‑related records** – keep records relating to property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition.  

These timelines apply unless a longer period is required for other purposes such as insurance or creditor requirements.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
The IRS guides you to choose the **cash method** if your business does **not have inventory**.  
In that case, income is reported when it is received and expenses are deducted when they are paid.  
This is the most common choice for many sole‑proprietor small businesses that keep only simple cash‑basis records.

> “Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method because they find it easier to keep cash method records.”  
> [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

If your business **does have inventory**, the general rule is that you must **use an accrual method** for the inventory portion, because accrual accounting properly matches sales with the cost of goods sold.  
You may still use the cash method for other non‑inventory items, but the overall method for inventory must be accrual.

> “If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for sales and purchases, unless you are a small business taxpayer.”  
> [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

A business qualifies as a **small‑business taxpayer** if it has average annual gross receipts of **$31 million or less for the prior three tax years** (indexed for inflation) and is not a tax shelter.

> “You qualify as a small business taxpayer if you (a) have average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the 3 prior tax years (indexed for inflation), and (b) are not a tax shelter.”
