runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes.  Because your shop is a private business that serves the public, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) classifies it as a **public accommodation**.  Under the ADA, you are required to eliminate physical barriers that are **“readily achievable”** without imposing an undue financial or technical burden.

* “Private businesses that provide goods or services to the public are called public accommodations… If you own, operate, lease, or lease‑to a business that serves the public, then you are covered by the ADA and have obligations for existing facilities… Existing facilities are not exempted by “grandfather provisions” that are often used by building‑code officials. …You must remove physical ‘barriers’ that are ‘readily achievable.’” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

If a barrier is not readily achievable, you must supply an **alternative** service (e.g., mobile service or a separate accessible entrance) that is likewise readily achievable. (ada_guide_small_business.pdf, pages 11‑13)

So, if the steps, entrances, parking, aisles, or counters can be made wheelchair‑accessible without excessive difficulty, you are required to do so.  If doing so is **not** readily achievable, you must provide an alternative service that is readily achievable.

runs.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
runs.answer:
**Getting a business up and running**

1. **Decide the legal form of your business** – apply the rules that the **IRS Guidance on “Determining Which Type of Business to Use”** explains:  
   * Sole proprietorship  
   * Partnership  
   * Limited‑liability company (LLC)  
   * Corporation  
   This decision affects your tax reporting, liability, and allowable deductions.  
   (irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 2‑3)

2. **Choose a name and register it if required** – If you operate as a sole proprietor or partnership and do not use the owner’s last name, you must file a fictitious‑name statement (or “doing‑business‑as”) with the state. For corporations or LLCs operating under a name other than the legal name, you must file an assumed‑business‑name statement with the Secretary of State.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)

3. **Apply for a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN)** – Most businesses will need an Employer Identification Number (EIN).  
   * Apply online for immediate issuance.  
   * Mailing or faxing Form SS‑4 takes at least 4 weeks.  
   * The EIN must be used on all returns, statements, and when another person uses your number.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)

4. **Set your accounting period (tax year)** – Choose either a calendar year (Jan 1 – Dec 31) or an alternative 12‑month period.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)

5. **Select an accounting method** – Decide between the *cash method* (expenses when paid, income when received) or the *accrual method* (expenses and income when incurred). The choice determines how you record liabilities, receivables, and depreciation.  
   

---

**Keeping your taxes organized**

| What to keep | Why they matter | Where to find the rule |
|--------------|-----------------|------------------------|
| **Supporting documents** (sales slips, invoices, receipts, bank deposits, canceled checks) | They back every entry in your books and prove the amounts reported on tax returns. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 12 |
| **Business books or journal entries** | They summarize every transaction and provide the basis for income statements, balance sheets, and cash‑flow statements. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 12‑13 |
| **Record‑keeping system (paper or electronic)** | All electronic systems must replicate the accuracy and legibility of hard‑copy books. The IRS may test the system. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 12‑13 |
| **Retention period** | Keep records for the period of limitations on the tax year they support: 3 years for most returns; 4 years for employment‑tax records. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 16 |
| **Year‑end reports** – income statement, balance sheet, cash‑flow, and notes – for managing the business, loan applications, and audit readiness | These documents also complement the **SBA business‑plan** and provide lenders or investors the financial snapshot they need. | sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 16 |

---

**Tax filing basics**

* **Income‑tax return** – As a sole proprietor, file **Form 1040 with Schedule C** (profit or loss from business). As a partnership, LLC, or corporation, use the appropriate form (e.g., 1040‑S, 1120, 1065).  
* **Self‑employment tax** – The same Schedule C returns automatically calculate the SE tax (Form SE).  
* **Estimated payments** – If you expect to owe more than $1 000, make quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040‑ES).  
* **Employment‑tax forms** – If you hire people, you must report wages and payroll taxes (Forms 941, 940, etc.).  
* **Information‑return forms** – Payees of over $600 must receive Form 1099‑MISC, W‑2 for employees, etc.  

(Full list of required federal tax forms and deadlines can be found in **Publication 334 – “Tax Guide for Small Business”**, Chapter 1.)

---

**Putting it all together**

1. Draft a **business plan** (SBA guide – page 4) covering purpose, market, operations, and finances.  
2. File the required state and federal registrations (name, EIN, etc.).  
3. Set up a simple **single‑entry or double‑entry bookkeeping system** (IRS guidance – page 15).  
4. Keep all **supporting documents, journals, ledgers, and bank reconciliations** and store them for the mandated period (IRS – page 12‑16).  
5. Use the records to prepare the required **tax returns** each year, cross‑check them with the financial statements in your plan, and file electronically when convenient (IRS e‑file).

These steps, taken together, provide a clear pathway from the initial idea to a fully organized tax‑ready small business.

runs.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
runs.answer:
**What you need to track for your taxes**

| Item | Why it matters (source) | Document & page |
|------|-------------------------|-----------------|
| **Income receipts (sales, services, rents, interests, etc.)** | Every dollar of income you receive is a taxable event.  You must report it on the appropriate schedule (e.g., Schedule C for sole‑proprietors). | *Publication 334 – Chapter 1, “Filing and Paying Business Taxes,” page 9‑10 |
| **Business‑related expenses** – e.g., rent, utilities, supplies, insurance, software, marketing, employee wages | These are deductible, provided they are ordinary and necessary. | *Publication 334 – Chapter 8, “Business Expenses,” page 32 |
| **Payroll documents (W‑2s, 1099‑NEC, 1099‑MISC, etc.)** | Required for reporting employee compensation and independent‑contractor payments. | *Publication 583 – “Business Taxes” section, page 8 |
| **Tax‑payable forms & deposits (Form 941/944 for employment tax, Form 720 for excise, Form 2909 for corporate tax, etc.)** | These prove you have paid the taxes you owe. | *Publication 334 – Chapter 1, “Filing and Paying Business Taxes,” pages 8‑10 |
| **Estimated tax payments (Form 1040‑ES)** | If you expect $1 000 or more of tax liability, you must make quarterly payments. | *Publication 334 – Chapter 1, “Estimated Tax,” page 1‑3 |
| **Record‑keeping logs (receipts, invoices, mileage logs, bank statements)** | IRS requires records that support income and deductions for the tax‑statements’ period. | *Publication 583 – “Recordkeeping,” page 16 |
| **Employee payroll records** | Required for preparing W‑2s, 941/944, FUTA, and withholding. | *Publication 583 – “Recordkeeping,” page 16 |

**What you need to track for travel expenses**

| Travel expense | What you can deduct / rule | Source & page |
|----------------|---------------------------|---------------|
| **Transportation (air, train, bus, car, taxi, limousine)** | Deduct the cost of travel between home and business destinations. | *Publication 334 – Chapter 8, “Travel and Meals,” page 40 |
| **Taxi, commuter bus, limousine fares** | Deduct fares between airport/station and hotel or between hotel and work location. | *Publication 334 – Chapter 8, “Travel and Meals,” page 40 |
| **Baggage / shipping of business items** | Deduct the cost of sending baggage, samples, or displays between work locations. | *Publication 334 – Chapter 8, “Travel and Meals,” page 40 |
| **Car or truck operating costs** | You may use the **actual‑expense method** (gas, oil, repairs, depreciation, etc.) or the **standard mileage rate** (70 ¢/mi for 2025).  P & T, tolls, parking, and rental‑car business portion are also deductible. | *Publication 334 – Chapter 8, “Travel and Meals,” page 41 |
| **Meals** | Deduct **50 %** of business‑related meal costs if the trip is overnight or long enough to sleep/rest. | *Publication 334 – Chapter 8, “Travel and Meals,” page 41 |
| **Lodging** | Deduct the full cost of a hotel or other overnight stay. | *Publication 334 – Chapter 8, “Travel and Meals,” page 41 |
| **Cleaning (dry‑cleaning, laundry)** | Deduct the business portion of such costs. | *Publication 334 – Chapter 8, “Travel and Meals,” page 41 |
| **Telephone & fax on the trip** | Deduct the business portion. | *Publication 334 – Chapter 8, “Travel and Meals,” page 41 |
| **Tips** | Deduct tips paid for any of the above services. | *Publication 334 – Chapter 8, “Travel and Meals,” page 41 |
| **Reimbursement of employees** | If you reimburse employees under an **accountable plan** or **non‑accountable plan**, the amount you deduct depends on the plan type. | *Publication 334 – Chapter 8, “Travel and Meals,” page 40‑41 |
| **Business Use of Home** | If you work from home to receive clients, you may have additional deductions (exclusive use, regular use, principal place of business). | *Publication 334 – Chapter 8, “Travel and Meals,” page 41 |
| **Record‑keeping** | Keep receipts, mileage logs, and detailed records that match the travel purpose. | *Publication 583 – “Recordkeeping,” page 16 |

---

### How to keep good records
1. **Maintain receipts and invoices** for every business expense, including travel.  
2. **Keep a mileage log** (date, purpose, miles traveled, business portion).  
3. **Save copies of W‑2s, 1099s, and payroll reports**.  
4. **Archive all evidence** (e.g., hotel receipts, meal bills, taxi invoices) for the period required by law.  

*Publication 583 – “Recordkeeping” (page 16)* specifically says you must keep records “as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code,” and that “you should keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return until the period of limitations for that return runs out.”

---

**Bottom line**  
Track all income and deductible business‑related expenses, keep thorough payroll and tax‑payment records, and for each business trip keep detailed logs and receipts for transportation, meals, lodging, and other associated costs. These documents enable you to claim the correct deductions, meet filing deadlines, and satisfy IRS record‑keeping requirements.

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
You **do need an employer identification number (EIN)** if your business is a partnership, corporation, LLC, or if you have employees or must file certain payroll or excise tax returns.  The IRS requires every business that fits one of those categories to obtain an EIN for use as a taxpayer‑identification number (TIN) when filing returns or reporting payments. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)

When you first file your business tax return you must also **choose an accounting method**.  The IRS offers two basic methods:

* **Cash method** – income is reported when received and expenses are deducted when paid.  
* **Accrual method** – income is reported when earned even if payment arrives later, and expenses are deducted when incurred.  

You select the method that best fits your business when you file your first Schedule C (or other business return). [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

runs.question: what health insurance plan should i buy for my staff
runs.answer:
The IRS guidance that is most relevant to deciding what type of health‑insurance plan to provide for your staff is found in the small‑business tax reference publications.

1. **Qualifications for a deductible “fringe benefit” health insurance plan**  
   The IRS defines the kinds of health insurance that can be treated as a fringe benefit (and therefore deducted as an ordinary and necessary business expense) on your tax return:
   > “Group‑hospitalization and medical insurance for employees, including long‑term care insurance.”  
   > “Insurance…related to your business.”  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=38)  

2. **Tax credit for small‑employer health‑insurance premiums**  
   If you pay premiums for a plan that covers certain employees, you may be eligible for the Small‑Employer Health Insurance Premiums Credit. The credit covers “the cost of certain health insurance coverage you provide to certain employees.”  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=20)

**What this means for you**

- Choose a **group‑hospitalization and medical insurance plan** that covers your employees (and, optionally, long‑term care). Group plans are the type of plan that IRS recognises as a deductible fringe benefit.
- Verify that the plan is a **group plan** (not an individual or commercial‑risk plan) so it qualifies for the deduction and for the Small‑Employer Health Insurance Premiums Credit.
- If you meet the eligibility criteria, you can claim the tax credit on Form 8941 (Credit for Small‑Employer Health Insurance Premiums).  

These documents do not prescribe a specific insurance carrier or policy; they only define the kinds of plans that are treated beneficially for tax purposes. You should therefore select a standard group hospitalization and medical insurance plan that meets your employees’ needs, and then verify the eligibility of that plan for the tax deductions and credits noted above.
